claims.text: AlCrFeNiSi powder is suitable as feedstock for additively manufactured miniature components.
Reducing laser power while increasing scan speed lowers the net thermal input in LPBF.
Low-energy-density LPBF reduces residual thermal stresses relative to conventional high-thermal-load LPBF.
Low-energy-density LPBF mitigates microstructural defects relative to conventional high-thermal-load LPBF.
Low-energy-density LPBF simplifies processing relative to conventional high-thermal-load LPBF.
Lower energy input reduces thermal gradients and moderates cooling rates during LPBF.
Reduced thermal gradients and moderated cooling rates produce a refined microstructure with fewer defects.
Lower net energy input confines the LPBF melt pool.
Decreased thermal gradients reduce the development of residual stresses.
Lower net energy input reduces defect formation.
Reduced residual stresses and defect formation improve mechanical integrity.
Lower-energy-density LPBF decreases the need for complex post-processing.
Low-energy-density LPBF components will have enhanced tensile properties relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load LPBF conditions.
Conventional high-energy-density LPBF parameters generate high thermal loads and associated microstructural issues.
The proposed hypothesis applies to LPBF miniature-component geometries typically under 10 mm.
Results from miniature AlCrFeNiSi components may not extend to larger geometries or fundamentally different alloy systems.
